title: 1947 BOAC Douglas C-47 crash
summary: BOAC Douglas C-47A G-AGJX, operating a scheduled international flight to West Africa via France, was diverted multiple times due to poor weather. After attempting to land at Bordeaux and Toulouse, the pilot decided to return to England as fuel was running short. The aircraft crashed into Barley Hill at Stowting, Kent while attempting to land at Lympne Airport. The aircraft struck the ground at a shallow angle, bounced 50 yards and crashed into trees.
probable_cause: The aircraft was diverted due to poor weather preventing landing at Bordeaux and other planned alternates. With fuel running short after multiple diversion attempts, the pilot attempted to land at Lympne Airport. The aircraft crashed into terrain during the landing approach. The Public Inquiry concluded mechanical failure was not the cause of the accident.

The pilot was running short of fuel and decided to return to England after diverting from Bordeaux.
After diverting from Bordeaux and requesting weather for Toulouse, the aircraft turned on heading back to England but then changed course for Paris.
The aircraft crashed into Barley Hill at Stowting while attempting to land at Lympne, indicating descent below safe altitude.
The aircraft crashed into Barley Hill, Hammond's Farm at Stowting, struck the ground at a shallow angle, bounced 50 yards and crashed into trees.

title: Eastern Air Lines 665

route.to_name: Smith Reynolds Airport, Winston-Salem, North Carolina

location.name: Providence Church, Grayson County near Galax

summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 665 crashed on 12 January 1947 near Galax, Virginia. The Douglas C-49-DO deviated from its course during a rainstorm, struck high ground, and burned. The pilot radioed at 0114 hours that he was five miles southeast of the field at 7,000 feet but this was erroneous navigation. The Civil Aeronautics Board concluded the pilot attempted a descent without positively determining aircraft position, with erroneous calculations on at least two occasions leading him to believe the aircraft was farther south than actually the case.
probable_cause: The action of the pilot in attempting a let-down without having positively determined the position of the aircraft. A contributing factor was the erroneous navigation of the pilot which on at least two occasions led him to believe that he was farther south than he actually was.

All 16 passengers and 6 crew members on board died. The probable cause was determined to be failure to remove the gust locks that had secured the aircraft's elevators while parked.

title: United Airlines 521
summary: United Air Lines Flight 521, a Douglas DC-4 from LaGuardia Airport, failed to become airborne on 29 May 1947 while attempting takeoff on runway 18. The aircraft overran the end of the runway, ripped through the airport fence onto traffic on the Grand Central Parkway, and slammed into an embankment before plunging into a pond and exploding. Ten people escaped the flaming wreckage; only five survived. It was the worst commercial aviation disaster in United States history at the time.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board determined the probable cause was either the failure of the pilot to release the gust lock before takeoff, or the decision to discontinue the takeoff because of apprehension resulting from rapid use of a short runway under calm wind conditions. Initial reports suggested wind shear may have been a factor, with a wind shift of almost unbelievable suddenness occurring during takeoff.

All 25 people on board were killed, making it Iceland's deadliest aviation accident at the time.

title: Pennsylvania Central Airlines 410
summary: Pennsylvania Central Airlines Flight 410, a Douglas DC-4, crashed into Lookout Rock in the West Virginia Blue Ridge Mountains at approximately 1,425 feet elevation while descending for Washington DC. All 50 passengers and crew were killed. The aircraft encountered thunderstorm weather, and the crew requested an alternate route requiring descent from 7,000 to 2,500 feet. The investigation found the pilot had erred in descending below the minimum altitude without adequate visual references and that ATC and the dispatcher provided an inappropriate clearance for an airway without established minimum altitude.
probable_cause: The pilot had erred in descending below the minimum altitude for which the flight had received clearance without adequate ground references. Contributing fault was assigned to Airway Traffic Control and the PCA dispatcher for providing an inappropriate clearance.

title: Pan Am 121
summary: A Lockheed L-049 Constellation suffered engine failure during cruise flight from Karachi to Istanbul, leading to overheating of remaining engines. One of the remaining engines then caught fire, which spread to the aircraft and caused structural damage. The burning magnesium parts separated from the aircraft, leaving it unable to maintain altitude, and it crashed in the Syrian desert at 4 miles from Mayadin. Fifteen people were killed.
probable_cause: Engine failure in the number one engine due to exhaust rocker arm fault. The crew elected to continue to Istanbul rather than divert to nearby airfields, causing the remaining engines to overheat. A subsequent engine fire spread to the aircraft structure, causing loss of altitude capability.

title: Dakota VT-CLA
summary: A Douglas C-47 chartered from India's Kalinga Airlines carrying medical supplies for the Indonesian independence government was shot down by two Dutch Curtiss P-40 Kittyhawk fighter aircraft as it approached the airfield at Yogyakarta. The P-40s destroyed the left engine, causing the aircraft to dive and crash into a tree and paddy field, with all but one occupant killed.
probable_cause: The aircraft was deliberately shot down by Dutch P-40 Kittyhawks during the Indonesian National Revolution. Although the Dutch initially denied involvement, investigation and witness testimony confirmed that the Kittyhawks attacked the aircraft and caused the crash.

title: BSAA Star Dust accident
summary: Star Dust, an Avro Lancastrian on charter from Buenos Aires to Santiago, crashed into Mount Tupungato at 15,000 feet after penetrating the poorly understood jet stream. The crew, believing they had cleared the mountain range at 24,000 feet and monitoring their calculated ground speed as exceeding their actual speed due to a headwind, descended into cloud-covered peaks they could not see. The aircraft hit the mountain at cruising speed with undercarriage retracted, indicating controlled flight into terrain. The wreckage was not found for 51 years, emerging from the Tupungato Glacier.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from controlled flight into terrain caused by navigational error. The crew mistakenly believed they had already cleared the Andes mountains and commenced descent when they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast. This navigational error was likely caused by the crew's unfamiliarity with the jet stream, which produced an unexpected headwind that reduced their ground speed below their calculated assumptions, making them believe they were further west than they actually were.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed into Mount Tupungato at approximately 15,000 feet altitude, striking the mountain while in controlled flight with engines running near cruising speed and undercarriage retracted.

The crew mistakenly assumed their ground speed to be faster than it really was and deduced that they had already safely crossed the Andes, whereas they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast and approaching the cloud-enshrouded Tupungato Glacier at high speed.
In the absence of visual sightings of the ground due to heavy clouds, the crew did not maintain awareness of their actual position relative to terrain.
Heavy clouds blocked visibility of the ground during the final portion of Star Dust's flight, preventing visual confirmation of position or terrain avoidance.
The jet stream phenomenon was not well understood in 1947, and the aircraft's navigation systems did not account for wind direction changes with altitude that the crew could not observe.

events.text: Aircraft cruising at 24,000 feet to cross Andes mountain range between Buenos Aires and Santiago.
Aircraft entered jet stream zone with headwind component, reducing actual ground speed significantly below crew's calculated assumptions.
Crew, mistakenly believing they had already cleared the mountain peaks, began descent toward Santiago.
Aircraft descended into cloud layers obscuring the cloud-covered Tupungato Glacier ahead, with no visual references available.

Aircraft impacted Mount Tupungato at high speed while in controlled flight, burying itself in snow and ice; the last Morse code transmission STENDEC was received by Santiago airport control tower four minutes before planned landing.

notes: Wreckage discovered in 1998 and 2000 in Tupungato Glacier at 15,000 feet elevation after 51+ years; previously missing.
The final Morse code transmission STENDEC has never been satisfactorily explained and remains a historical mystery.

title: United Air Lines 608
summary: In-flight fire in the baggage compartment developed from overfilled fuel tank venting into the cabin heater system. As the aircraft descended toward Bryce Canyon Airport, pieces of the aircraft including the right wing fell off. The crew was unable to maintain control in canyon gusts despite being only 10 feet above ground, and the aircraft crashed on National Park Service land. The fire and structural damage resulted from a design flaw in the cabin heater intake scoop placement relative to the fuel tank vent.
probable_cause: Design flaw: a cabin heater intake scoop was positioned too close to the number 3 alternate fuel tank air vent. When the fuel tank was overfilled during routine transfer, excess fuel was sucked into the cabin heater system and ignited. Contributing factors were inadequate crew training about the danger and failure to halt the fuel transfer before tank overflow.

title: 1947 Oregon Beechcraft Bonanza crash
summary: On 28 October 1947, a Beechcraft Bonanza piloted by veteran pilot Cliff Hogue departed Klamath Falls at 10:00 pm in stormy weather conditions carrying Oregon Governor Earl Snell, Senate President Marshall Cornett, and Secretary of State Robert Farrell to a hunting trip. The aircraft descended into mountainous terrain at 6,000 feet elevation and crashed 2 miles west of Dog Lake in dense Ponderosa pine forest. All four occupants were killed.

title: General Leclerc's aviation accident
summary: A B-25 Mitchell transport aircraft carrying General Leclerc and 12 others departed Villacoublay for North Africa and crashed near Colomb-Béchar in bad weather conditions with sandstorms and strong headwinds. The aircraft had been modified by the French Air Force with an internal bunk at the rear, creating weight and balance issues. Investigation concluded the crash resulted from the aircraft being at too low an airspeed in the poor weather conditions, with passengers moving toward the rear of the aircraft inducing a flat spin.
probable_cause: The official report concluded the crash was due to recklessness of pilot François Delluc and persistence of General Leclerc in ignoring unfavorable weather conditions. Later analysis indicated dangerous modification with an added bunk likely caused a counterbalance, and passengers moving to the rear combined with reduced speed in weather conditions induced a flat spin.
